meta.titre: Magnetic field patterns: rules for drawing field lines
meta.sous_theme: Field lines, neutral points and solenoids

sections.contenu_markdown: A hunter in the forest of the East Region carries a compass and trusts its needle to point north even when he cannot see the sun. In the school laboratory, iron filings sprinkled on a card above a magnet line up in curved patterns that show where the magnetic force acts. The GCE regularly asks you to draw, in your answer booklet, the magnetic field pattern of a magnet or of a coil, with the correct arrows. Here you will learn the rules for drawing field lines and how to describe the most common patterns in words, so that you can draw them correctly.

items: A magnet has a north pole (N) and a south pole (S); like poles repel and unlike poles attract.
A magnetic field is the region around a magnet in which a magnetic force acts on a magnetic material or another magnet.
A plotting compass is a small magnet on a pivot; its north-seeking end points along the field.

sections.titre: Drawing and describing magnetic field patterns
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Direction of field lines.** A magnetic field line shows the path that a free north pole would follow. Outside a magnet, the lines go **from the north pole to the south pole**, and each line carries an arrow in that direction. Inside the magnet they continue from S to N, so every line is a closed loop.

**Rules for drawing field lines.**

1. Lines never cross each other, because the field has one direction at each point.
2. Lines are closest together where the field is strongest, which is at the poles. They spread out where the field is weak.
3. Lines leave and enter the pole faces at $90^\circ$ to the surface.
4. Lines are smooth curves that start and end on poles; they never stop in the middle of nowhere.

**Patterns to know.**

| Arrangement | Pattern of lines |
|---|---|
| Single bar magnet | lines leave N, curve round and return to S; the lines are closest at the two ends |
| Unlike poles facing (N opposite S) | lines run from N to S, nearly straight and parallel in the gap, so the field there is uniform; they bulge outward at the edges |
| Like poles facing (N opposite N) | lines leave both poles and are pushed apart; they bend away from each other, and there is a neutral point between the poles where the field is zero |
| Current-carrying coil (solenoid) | the same pattern as a bar magnet: straight parallel lines inside the coil, and loops outside from one end to the other |

**Earth's field.** The Earth behaves like a huge bar magnet. A compass needle points to the north because the end of the magnet near geographic north is a magnetic south pole.

variantes.nom: Plotting a field with a compass
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to describe how to find the field of a magnet in the laboratory.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Place the magnet on a sheet of paper and draw round it. Put a plotting compass near one pole and mark the positions of both ends of the needle. Move the compass so that its tail is on the last mark, and mark the new head. Repeat until you reach the other pole, then join the marks with a smooth line and add an arrow from N to S. Repeat from different starting points. Iron filings sprinkled on card show the pattern quickly but do not show the direction.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When field lines of two magnets meet, or when a question asks how to protect an instrument from a magnetic field.
variantes.contenu_markdown: A **neutral point** is a point where the fields of two magnets cancel and the resultant field is zero; a compass placed there points in no fixed direction. A ring of **soft iron** placed round an instrument shields it: the field lines pass through the iron instead of crossing the empty space, so the inside of the ring has almost no field.

variantes.nom: Field of a solenoid and polarity
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question shows a coil carrying current and asks which end is north.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Look at one end of the coil. If the current flows **anticlockwise** round that end, it is a **north** pole; if it flows **clockwise**, it is a **south** pole. A magnet moved towards a coil induces a current in the coil whose field opposes the motion, so the end of the coil nearest the approaching north pole becomes a north pole.

sections.enonce_markdown: Two identical bar magnets lie on a sheet of paper $6\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart, with their north poles facing each other. Describe how you would find the magnetic field pattern with a plotting compass, describe the pattern you would obtain, and locate the neutral point.

etapes.action: Mark the magnets and set up the compass.
etapes.justification: The outline and the poles must be fixed on the paper so that the pattern can be related to the magnets.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Draw round each magnet and label the N poles. Place the compass next to the first N pole and mark the two ends of the needle.

etapes.justification: The needle lies along the field, so successive positions follow a field line.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Move the compass so that its tail is at the last head mark, mark the new head, and continue. Join the points with a smooth curve and add an arrow away from the N pole.

etapes.action: Repeat and describe the whole pattern.
etapes.justification: Several lines from each N pole are needed to see the pattern as a whole.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Lines leave each N pole, curve away from the other magnet and do not cross. The lines from the two poles do not join across the gap; they turn away from each other.

etapes.justification: The two equal N poles push the compass equally in opposite directions on the line between them.
etapes.resultat_markdown: At the midpoint, $\dfrac{6}{2} = 3\ \mathrm{cm}$ from each pole, the field is zero. The compass needle there points in no fixed direction.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The pattern shows lines repelling each other with a neutral point $3\ \mathrm{cm}$ from each pole, midway along the line between the two north poles.

items.erreur_markdown: "I drew the arrows from the south pole to the north pole outside the magnet."
items.pourquoi_faux: The direction of the field is the direction in which a north pole would move. Outside the magnet, this is from N to S.
items.correction_markdown: Put arrows on the outside lines pointing away from N and towards S.

items.erreur_markdown: "I drew two lines crossing at one point to show a strong field."
items.pourquoi_faux: Lines never cross, because a compass at that point would have to point two ways at once. A strong field is shown by lines close together.
items.correction_markdown: Draw lines that bunch together at the poles and never meet each other.

items.erreur_markdown: "The field lines from the N pole stop in the air, halfway to the S pole."
items.pourquoi_faux: Field lines are continuous. Each one leaves a N pole and arrives at a S pole (or loops back through the magnet).
items.correction_markdown: Draw each line from N all the way to S.

items.erreur_markdown: "With two north poles facing, the lines join up and run from one magnet to the other."
items.pourquoi_faux: Lines run from N to S. Between two N poles they push apart, which creates a neutral point. The joining pattern is the one for unlike poles.
items.correction_markdown: For like poles, draw lines bending away from each other, and mark the neutral point midway between.

items.erreur_markdown: "Iron filings show the direction of the field."
items.pourquoi_faux: Filings line up along the field, but they do not tell which way along the line the field points.
items.correction_markdown: Use a plotting compass for the direction, or draw arrows from N to S.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) State the direction of the magnetic field outside a bar magnet. (b) A plotting compass is placed beside the south pole of a bar magnet. Which way does the north-seeking end of the needle point? (c) What does it mean when field lines are close together?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Outside the magnet, the field points **from the north pole to the south pole**.

(b) The north end of the needle points **towards the south pole of the bar magnet**, since unlike poles attract.

(c) The field is **strong** where the lines are close together, as at the poles.

items.enonce_markdown: A north pole of one bar magnet faces the south pole of another, $4\ \mathrm{cm}$ apart. (a) Describe the field lines in the gap. (b) Describe what happens at the edges of the gap. (c) Describe the position and direction of a compass needle placed in the middle of the gap.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The lines run from the N pole to the S pole and are nearly **straight and parallel**, so the field in the gap is nearly uniform.

(b) At the edges the lines **bulge outward** and then curve round.

(c) The needle lies along the lines of the gap: its north-seeking end points **towards the S pole** (away from the N pole).

items.enonce_markdown: (a) A current flows anticlockwise round the left end of a long solenoid, as seen from the left. State the polarity of the left end and the direction of the field inside the coil. (b) Explain how a soft iron ring protects a watch from the field of a nearby magnet. (c) A north pole of a magnet is pushed towards the right end of a coil joined to a sensitive meter. State the polarity of the coil's right end while the pole is approaching.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Anticlockwise current means the left end is a **north pole**. Inside the coil the field runs from the south end to the north end, that is **from right to left**.

(b) The soft iron is easily magnetised, so the field lines pass through the iron instead of crossing the space inside the ring. The field inside the ring, where the watch is, is almost zero.

(c) The induced current opposes the approach of the north pole, so the right end becomes a **north pole** and repels the incoming north pole.

items_markdown: Outside a magnet, field lines run from the north pole to the south pole; each line is a closed loop and carries an arrow.
Field lines never cross; they are closest at the poles, where the field is strongest, and they leave the pole faces at right angles.
Unlike poles facing give straight parallel lines in the gap; like poles facing give lines pushed apart and a neutral point between them.
A plotting compass gives the direction of the field; iron filings show the pattern but not the direction.
A solenoid has the same field as a bar magnet: anticlockwise current makes the end a north pole, clockwise a south pole.
